PhD 11 - Thermo-hygral-mechanical modelling and optimisation of dry-out and early-age behaviour in castable refractory linings
A 36 Months PhD starting in October 2026 and supervised between UMINHO (Portugal) and RHIM-Leoben (Austria)
PhD11 will develop and validate a thermo-hygro-mechanical finite element modelling framework for the dry-out of castable ladle linings, comparing natural and accelerated drying schedules. The project will instrument laboratory specimens, a biaxial press and a pilot ladle to monitor moisture transport, temperature and internal stress. It will model damage caused by pore pressure, early-age creep and microcracking, and assess how these phenomena influence later corrosion and degradation.
PhD11 is closely connected to PhD06, PhD14 and PhD15. Its thermo-hygro-mechanical modelling of dry-out and early-age behaviour provides inputs for digital twin development and operational decision support, while also benefiting from materials knowledge on binder systems and castable design. Its results are also relevant for sustainability and traceability by contributing drying-phase performance indicators.
Master’s level in Engineering or similar field. Candidates should have strong understanding of constitutive modelling and numerical skills in multiphysics environments. A solid background in programming in object-oriented languages such as python or others. Excellent oral and written communication skills in English are required.

Dabei bringst du dich in ein Forschungsthema ein, das Computer Vision, maschinelles Lernen, geometrische Optimierung und automobile Messtechnik verbindet. 
 Was erwartet dich? 
 Du gestaltest die Konzeption und Umsetzung einer modularen Pipeline für katalogbasiertes, markerloses Fahrzeugtracking mit. 
 Gemeinsam mit dem Team trägst du zur Entwicklung eines generalisierbaren Fahrzeugdetektors bei. 
 Du beteiligst dich an der Erforschung robuster Pose-Estimation statt fahrzeugspezifischer Oberflächenmerkmale. 
 Im Rahmen der Forschung unterstützt du die Untersuchung geometrischer Verfahren. 
 Zur Validierung der geschätzten Fahrzeugpose unterstützt du den Abgleich mit unabhängigen, metrologisch belastbaren Ground-Truth-Daten und die Bewertung anhand realer Toleranzen. 
 Bei der Publikation der Forschungsergebnisse und dem Aufbau interner Expertise für markerloses Augmented-Reality-Tracking bringst du dich aktiv ein.

boards-phd:linkedin:4493628143.desc: Job Description Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is an inherited retinal disease that progressively damages photoreceptors, the light-sensitive cells responsible for vision. Although new treatments, including gene therapies, are emerging, monitoring disease progression remains challenging because current clinical imaging techniques cannot always detect subtle changes in these cells. Adaptive optics imaging enables visualisation of individual cone photoreceptors in the living human eye. However, in patients with RP, these cells often appear irregular, with changes in their shape, reflectivity, and […] tial organisation. This makes automated detection and quantification difficult, while the relationship between these abnormalities and visual function is not yet fully understood. Within the AICON project, Erasmus MC and the Rotterdam Eye Hospital aim to address these challenges by developing AI-based methods to automatically detect, quantify, and characterise cone photoreceptors in patients with RP. By combining adaptive optics imaging with Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) and microperimetry, the project will investigate how microscopic changes relate to retinal structure, visual function, and disease progression. The ultimate goal is to develop reliable imaging biomarkers to support disease monitoring and future clinical trials. As a PhD candidate, you will play a central role in this project, developing and validating AI and image analysis methods for detecting and characterising cone photoreceptors in diseased retinas. You will work with advanced retinal imaging datasets and collaborate closely with imaging researchers and ophthalmologists to investigate how cellular abnormalities relate to disease progression and patients' vision. Responsibilities Contribute to data curation, quality assessment, and annotation in collaboration with a technical ophthalmic assistant and clinical specialists. Develop and validate AI-based methods for automated cone detection, phenotyping, …

boards-phd:linkedin:4493632261.desc: Every satellite we launch shares space with defunct spacecraft, spent rocket stages and fragments from past collisions. Tracking all of it is one of the big challenges for keeping space usable. What if satellites already in orbit could help? Every satellite carries a star tracker, a small camera that steers by the stars, and those cameras also catch passing debris. AstroSweep aims to turn them into debris detectors, with artificial intelligence picking out the objects that matter. We're looking for a research fellow to help build it. At FEUP – Faculty of Engineering, University of Porto , you'll design and develop the pipeline that detects, catalogues and analyses orbital debris. You'll take it from the state of the art all the way to a working, validated system, as part of a project co-funded by the EU through COMPETE 2030. This is for you if: ✅ You're enrolled in a PhD in Engineering Physics or a related field (this is only required when signing the contract) ✅ You hold a master's degree in Engineering Physics, Computer Engineering or a related field ⭐ You have experience in AI, or a strong drive to apply it to real space data 📅 Apply by 30 November 2026 (23:59, Lisbon time) 🔗 https://www.apply.up.pt/procedure/i3g6p222q644rfjm Ref. at-nl:365796.desc:
What happens when the Internet fails? 
 Job description 
What happens when the Internet fails?
What happens when a submarine cable is cut? When satellites lose contact with one another? Or when a cyberattack disrupts the networks we depend on every day? The Internet is remarkably resilient, but it is far from invulnerable. As our dependence on digital infrastructure grows, so does the need to understand where it is vulnerable, how failures spread, and what we can do about them.
These are some of the questions we want to explore in RESILIOUS.
We are bringing together 15 PhD researchers and a […] requirements 
We welcome applications from curious and motivated people from around the world. You don't need to know everything about your chosen research topic before starting your PhD. We're looking for people who enjoy tackling difficult problems, asking questions, learning new things, and working with others. Different positions call for different skills and backgrounds, so have a look at the individual vacancies to see which ones interest you.

 No PhD yet: You must not already hold a doctoral degree at the time of recruitment.

Pour répondre à ce problème, des approches logicielles et matérielles sont de plus en plus adoptées. D’un côté, les accélérateurs matériels (par exemple, FPGA, TPU, GPU) permettent d’optimiser le calcul matriciel et traiter en parallèle le calcul divisé en plusieurs sous-tâches. De l’autre côté, les techniques logicielles (par exemple, élagage ou quantification), permettent de réduire la taille du réseau. boards-phd:indeed:a77c5a469428b9bb.title: PhD position: Safe deployment of semi-autonomous AI in radiology
boards-phd:indeed:a77c5a469428b9bb.desc: Functiebeschrijving Every day, radiologists review hundreds of scans to find out whether a patient has cancer. The number of scans keeps growing, but the number of radiologists does not. AI can help. For prostate cancer, AI systems can now read MRI scans about as well as experienced radiologists. Yet today a radiologist still checks every scan, so the AI saves little time. That could change if AI were allowed to handle the clear-cut cases on its own, leaving radiologists more time for the difficult ones. But a hospital is not a static environment. New scanners are installed, scan settings […] ge and the patient population shifts over time. Each of these changes can make an AI system less accurate without anyone noticing. Radiologists who work with AI every day may also start to trust it more than they should. European law now requires hospitals and manufacturers to keep monitoring AI once it is in use, but nobody has yet shown how to do that reliably in practice. In this PhD project, funded by Stichting Hanarth Fonds, you will work out how to monitor AI safely in daily clinical practice, using prostate MRI as a starting point. You will: develop and validate statistical methods that detect drops in AI performance early, using a multicenter dataset of more than 10,000 prostate MRI examinations collected over twelve years; design and run an international reader study that measures how strongly AI advice influences radiologists; translate these findings into a monitoring protocol together with international experts, aligned with the EU AI Act; test the protocol prospectively in a multicenter study at UMCG and Radboudumc on more than 500 new examinations, in parallel with routine care; publish your work in international journals and present it at conferences, leading to a PhD thesis. You will work in a multidisciplinary team of radiologists, AI researchers and legal experts from UMCG, Radboudumc and the University of Groningen. The work combines technical depth with …

The BRIDGE-AI doctoral network is employing 15 ambitious doctoral candidates at various locations in Europe (Finland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Germany, Switzerland and Austria). We are currently inviting applications for the last 3 open PhD positions, located in Germany and Finland (see below). The aim of the BRIDGE-AI network is to develop new and trustworthy AI methods for longitudinal neuroimage analysis, helping clinical experts assess temporal changes in patients with chronic brain disorders. More information about the project is available from the BRIDGE-AI website .
DC1: Deep learning for cortical surface-based analyses (Bonn, Germany)
Employer: German Center for Neurodegenerative Diseases (DZNE)
Main supervisor: Prof. Dr. Martin Reuter

Are you passionate about advancing neuroscience and clinical applications through cutting-edge AI technology? Do you want to contribute to tools that can transform how we understand brain function, study neurological diseases, and evaluate large-scale population studies? Join us to develop innovative AI methods for cortical surface modeling – an essential foundation for modern neuroimaging research.

Why This Matters: The cerebral cortex, with its intricate folds and complex structure, holds key insights into brain health and disease. Accurate modeling and analysis of the cortical surface enable breakthroughs in understanding brain development, detecting abnormalities, and tracking disease progression. Your work will help build powerful AI tools that can improve diagnosis, guide treatment strategies, and push the boundaries of neuroscience research.
In this PhD project, you will:
Develop advanced AI methods to segment brain cortical atlases based on surface data, moving beyond traditional approaches.
Create algorithms to detect anomalies on the cortical surface, such as Focal Cortical Dysplasia (FCD), aiding early diagnosis of neurological conditions.
Innovate deep learning solutions for longitudinal surface extraction, tracking brain changes over time with unprecedented accuracy.
Implement state-of-the-art deep learning techniques for cross-subject and cross-time surface registration.
Thoroughly validate your methods to ensure broad applicability in neuroimaging workflows.

Your contributions will elevate the accuracy, reliability, and generalizability of cortical surface analysis, setting new standards for the field. They will generate impact through their possible integration into widely used neuroimaging pipelines such as FastSurfer and FreeSurfer.

What We Offer: We are the developers of FastSurfer and co-developers of FreeSurfer , world-leading open-source neuroimage analysis pipelines. We are experts in developing advanced deep-learning methods for medical image processing. At our lab you will have access to excellent supervision and to a powerful computational environment, including a high-performance cluster with close to one hundred NVIDIA 32GB GPUs and four dedicated servers reserved exclusively for our group, each with 8 GPUs (32-40GB RAM each). Furthermore, we offer research stays at world-renowned institutions, including the Martinos Center at MGH and Harvard Medical School, Boston USA, as well as Icometrix, Belgium. We provide a dynamic, collaborative research environment with mentorship from experts in AI, neuroimaging, and clinical neuroscience.
You hold a strong background in computer science, biomedical engineering, applied mathematics, or a related field.
You have experience in machine learning and deep learning with applications in medical imaging or neuroscience.
You are motivated to work on impactful research that bridges AI development with real-world neurological applications.
You possess solid programming skills (Python and PyTorch) and optimally have worked with geometric representations, such as triangle meshes.
Experience with brain MRI data, or longitudinal analysis is a plus but not mandatory.
If you’re eager to push the frontiers of AI in neuroscience and contribute to transformative research with world-class collaborators and resources, we want to hear from you !
Foreseen secondments: For this PhD project, research visits are foreseen to:
Prof. Dr. Bruce Fischl (3 months) at LCN – Martinos Center for Biomedical Imaging / MGH / Harvard Medical School (Boston, USA) – core developer of FreeSurfer and world-renowned neuroimaging expert.
Dr. Dirk Smeets (1 month) at Icometrix (Leuven, Belgium) – industry leader on advanced methods for medical image analysis.
Dr. Theodor Rüber (8 months collaboration while at DZNE) at Translational NeuroImaging Lab, University Clinic Bonn (Bonn, Germany) – expert on clinical neuroimaging in epilepsy.
DC9: Interpretable prediction of gestational age from fetal brain MRI across institutions (Espoo, Finland)
PhD enrollment: Aalto University , Espoo, Finland
Main supervisor: prof. Koen Van Leemput

PhD project description: The assessment of whether a fetus is at the expected development stage is currently performed in a rather primitive fashion in the clinic: clinicians manually perform 2D measurements from fetal brain MRI scans, and compare those to normative growth curves to see whether development is delayed. In this PhD project, you will significantly advance this state of affairs by developing new probabilistic generative models of the developing neuroanatomy across gestational ages, and use those models to accurately estimate the gestational age from fetal MRI scans.

This is a highly relevant but also very ambitious project: In order to be fully clinically useful, the methods and tools that you will develop should work “out-of-the-box” on data that is acquired with different scanners, image resolutions, reconstruction algorithms and acquisition protocols. Furthermore, your models should encode the cause-effect relationship between gestational age and the acquired MRI scans, so that the obtained predictions are inherently interpretable for clinicians (for instance, by generating counterfactuals simulating a particular fetus’s neuroanatomy at different gestational ages). Once you are confident in the performance of your methods and tools, you should also apply them to large clinical datasets of both normal and abnormal brain development.

Your profile: This position requires strong skills in both math (e.g., linear algebra, Bayesian statistics) and coding (e.g., Python/NumPy, C++). Prior experience with medical imaging is not required.
Foreseen secondments: For this PhD project, research visits are foreseen to:
prof. Meritxell Bach Cuadra (9 months) at the University of Lausanne (Lausanne, Switzerland)
Dr. Tom Hilbert (2 months) at Siemens Healthineers (Lausanne, Switzerland)
DC14: Longitudinal progression markers derived from WM and GM alterations in different epilepsy phenotypes (Espoo, Finland)
PhD enrollment: Aalto University , Espoo, Finland
Main supervisors: prof. Koen Van Leemput & Dr. Richard McKinley (Bern, Switzerland)

Clinical Problem : Among patients who present with a first seizure, approximately 45% will have a further seizure within the next five years. Identifying which patients are likely to have recurrent seizures is therefore vitally important, since early treatment can dramatically improve the lives of patients with epilepsy and spare them from further neurological deficits brought on by repeated seizures.

Structural brain lesions are the most common cause of epileptic seizures, but the mere presence of a lesion is not predictive of epilepsy: the size and location of the lesion, and its proximity to the grey matter, are critical factors. Similarly, while loss of grey matter is seen in all epilepsy patients over time, specific patterns of grey-matter atrophy can be associated to different epilepsy subtypes. Identifying these patterns in a timely manner has the potential to drive patient treatment.

Your solution : In this PhD project you will develop methods to link patterns of grey- and white-matter alterations to epilepsy subtypes and to distinguish epilepsy patients from those with epilepsy mimics. You will benchmark and extend existing segmentation methods for quantifying white matter lesions and grey matter atrophy, and establish baselines for linking alterations and disease, such as lesion-symptom mapping and structural covariance networks. You will then explore how generative modeling can be harnessed to translate patterns of brain alteration into low-dimensional latent codes which capture the essence of a patient’s deviation from normal brain appearance, and harness these codes to better estimate a patient’s risk of receiving a definitive epilepsy diagnosis. The methods developed will be based on data from, and have direct application in, ongoing studies at the University Hospital Bern and across Switzerland, which aim to identify patients at high risk of developing epilepsy after a first seizure, and to study the effects of epilepsy over time on the structure, function and metabolism of the brain.
Foreseen secondments: For this PhD project, research visits are foreseen to:
Prof Roland Wiest & Dr. Richard McKinley, Inselspital, University Hospital Bern, Switzerland (10 months across 3 visits)
Dr Ankur Sharma, Bayer (Berlin, Germany) (2 months)

CAVECORE Continuous, Automated Validation, and Evaluation of Cognitive Robots in Open-Ended Environments (CAVECORE). "> Funded by The European Union under The Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) Doctoral Networks programme Grant Agreement No. 101227310.

CAVECORE (Continuous, Automated Validation, and Evaluation of Cognitive Robots in Open-Ended Environments) is a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Doctoral Network that trains the next generation of researchers to advance cognitive robotics —robots that can interact, learn, and adapt to open-ended real-world environments. The network addresses one of the central challenges in AI-enabled robotics: evaluating and validating the quality , safety , and reliability of such robots in a systematic and trustworthy manner.

Doctoral Candidates in CAVECORE will follow an interdisciplinary training program that combines expertise in robotics and AI (e.g., learning-enabled manipulation, control, and human-robot interaction) with cutting-edge validation and evaluation methods (e.g., automated testing, diagnosis, analysis, and AI metrology). They will develop novel approaches that make evaluability-by-design a core part of the robot development process, ensuring that cognitive robots provide continuous evidence of their performance and can adapt to evolving societal, ethical, and legal requirements such as those set out in the EU AI Act. By engaging in secondments across leading academic and industrial partners , DCs gain hands-on experience, professional skills, and unique career perspectives. They will be prepared to lead innovation in robotics that is not only technically advanced but also economically viable and socially responsible, with applications ranging from agile production to logistics and maritime robotics.

This Doctoral Network will provide its Doctoral Candidates with a rigorous training in solving complex problems characterised by many degrees of freedom and intrinsic noise, all of which arise in the context of biological systems and are key to functions as movement, growth and regulation. Each Doctoral Candidate will pursue research within one of the PhD Research Projects described below, utilising techniques from statistical and condensed matter physics to discover how collective phenomena emerge in biological systems from interactions between their component parts.

A distinctive feature of this Doctoral Network is that a novel combination of modelling and analysis techniques, which traditionally have each been applied in a specific problem domain, lies at the heart of each PhD research project. For this reason, Doctoral Candidates will each have two supervisors, one at the primary host institution (indicated in the panels below), and another at a second institution in the network, with a period of research at the second institution, fully funded by the programme, designed into the research projects. Some projects additionally feature secondments with our non-academic partners.

Full details of project goals, methodologies, hosting and secondment arrangements are provided within each description below. Recruitment is now completed with offers made to the successful candidates. All PhD projects are to begin on September 1st 2026 or as soon as possible thereafter.
Bayesian inference of active Brownian motion

For the study of motile cells and other self-propelled particles it is often key to extract quantitative features from trajectories of these particles, both to quantify experimental trajectories and to parametrise theoretical models.
Beyond the extensile/contractile dichotomy in active nematics
Active nematics is one of the most studied situations in active matter physics, both in theory and experiments.
The University of Edinburgh, United Kingdom
Bottom-up modelling of dense bacterial suspensions
Dense active suspensions, such as those formed by swarming bacteria, constitute a type of active matter that is particularly hard to model.
Collective tug-of-war dynamics: from molecular motors to ant groups
The emergence of directed transport as a collective behaviour of many microscopic constituents is a ubiquitous problem in the statistical physics of active particles.
The University of Edinburgh, United Kingdom
Control theory for topological active matter
Experimental techniques have demonstrated the ability to alter the collective dynamics of active systems with various types of external perturbations.
Defect dynamics in pulsating active matter

Some collective states in active matter exhibit topological properties through the formation of vortices and defects. In some living systems, defects have been shown to have important biological functions.
Dense active matter and the cage escape dynamics of active particles
Passive particles form amorphous solids or glasses at high densities. The same is true of active particles that model living matter such as confluent tissues.

The dynamics of the sperm flagellum has been recently studied with particular attention to its fluctuations. It has been found that the precision of the flagellar beating is close to that of an individual dynein motor powering its motion, which in turn is close to the bound dictated by the thermodynamic uncertainty relation.
NANOTEC-CNR/The Sapienza University of Rome, Italy
Elucidating the role of mechano-signalling feedback in dense cellular collectives

Collective tissue behaviour is inherently a multiscale phenomenon that is governed by complex biochemical and mechanical processes occurring simultaneously at the molecular, cellular, and tissue scales.
Exploring active field theories to unravel solidification of protein condensates

The spatial organisation of proteins into dense condensates, widely attributed to nonequilibrium phase separation, offers a route to recruit or sequester proteins involved in functions at the cellular level.
Growth of cells in viscoelastic medium

Typically, the complex environments in which living systems reside are viscoelastic fluids. For example, the extracellular matrix comprises cross-linked, semiflexible polymeric filaments that respond sensitively to even small stresses generated by cells.
Institute of Physical Chemistry Polish Academy of Sciences, Poland
Learning non-reciprocal interactions between migrating cells

Owing to their active nature, interactions between migrating cells can be non-reciprocal. However, the extent to which cells control their collective behaviour through non-reciprocal interactions remains unclear.
Active field theories are widely used to study collective effects in driven systems at all levels of organisation, allowing instabilities to pattern formation to be identified.
The University of Edinburgh, United Kingdom

While active matter theory has successfully advanced our understanding of the collective dynamics resulting from individual sources of activity, multiple active processes usually act in concert in real biological systems.
Max-Planck Institute for Dynamics and Self-Organization/University of Göttingen, Germany
Statistical mechanics of motility and growth within extracellular matrices

Collective cellular activity and self-organisation phenomena arising from non-equilibrium activity are ubiquitous in tissues and cellular aggregates. However, the relationship between individual properties and biological patterns remains unexplored.
The University of Leiden, The Netherlands

Decoding and designing biomolecular systems with hybrid DNA:RNA:protein nanotechnology

Our increasing knowledge of the fundamental mechanisms of life and the confluence of techniques are the basis for the development of novel life-inspired technologies. In recent years, notably in the development of COVID-19 vaccines, we have witnessed the pivotal role played by RNA in nanomedical advancements. At the same time, DNA nanotechnology has already proven to yield some of the most complex, yet well controlled, artificial biomolecular structures.

Taking these different ingredients together, our abilities of building bottom-up functional machines and biomolecular systems involving DNA, RNA and proteins are currently emerging quicker than ever before, with new prospects for drug design and delivery, biosensors, as well as complex biomolecular robots and materials.

To unlock the full potential for complex biosensing devices that modularly emulate life-like functions and interact in complex biomolecular environments, BioHYBRITE brings together a unique team of world leading academics in the forefront of relevant bottom-up hybrid nanotechnologies, through the EU Horizon Europe MSCA DN funding scheme (Grant Agreement Nr. 101227379).

Which positions are open, and when should I apply? Check the vacancy listings and individual doctoral project pages for open positions. Each university advertisement specifies its own application window, requirements and deadline.

How do I submit an application? Read the doctoral project page, then follow its link to the recruiting university’s official advertisement. Submit your application through the procedure specified there. Vacancies will also be advertised on EURAXESS. The EMANAIRE website provides information and links; it does not receive applications.

Can I apply to more than one project? Yes. You may apply to up to four EMANAIRE doctoral projects. Submit a separate application for each position. In each motivation or cover letter, briefly identify your other EMANAIRE applications, including any you intend to submit, using the project numbers or titles. Tailor each application to the project concerned.

What academic background do I need? We welcome applicants interested in the human and organisational implications of AI. Relevant backgrounds may include management, organisation studies, psychology, sociology, communication and information systems. Each project has its own academic, methodological and language requirements, and you must meet the host university’s doctoral admission requirements.

Can I apply if I am still completing my master’s degree? This depends on the university. Check its advertisement for when your qualifying degree must be completed and what evidence you should provide. Contact the recruiting university if you are unsure whether your expected graduation date meets its requirements.

Can applicants of any nationality apply? Yes. MSCA Doctoral Network positions are open to applicants of any nationality. You must also satisfy the mobility rule, doctoral-status condition and the recruiting university’s admission and employment requirements. Visa or residence-permit arrangements depend on your circumstances and the host country.

What is the MSCA mobility rule? In general, you must not have lived or carried out your main activity, such as work or study, in the recruiting country for more than 12 months in the 36 months immediately before recruitment. This is assessed separately for each recruiting country. The university will check your circumstances and any applicable exceptions; consult its advertisement for the full conditions.

Can I apply if I already have a doctorate? You must not hold a doctoral degree when recruited. Researchers who have successfully defended a doctoral thesis are also ineligible, even if the degree has not yet been formally awarded.

Which documents should I prepare? Follow the individual university advertisement. Requirements may include a CV, motivation letter, degree certificates and transcripts, references, a research proposal and evidence of MSCA eligibility. Proposal lengths and document formats differ between hosts. Use the official instructions for each application rather than one standard document package.

Are the positions funded, and how long do they last? The doctoral positions are supported through EMANAIRE’s MSCA funding. Salary, allowances, contract duration and any additional institutional funding are specified by each recruiting university. Check each advertisement for its own employment terms.

Where will I be based, and will I travel? You will be based at the host university listed for your project and join shared network activities. Planned secondments and academic visits provide experience in other research and professional settings. The arrangements for your position, including travel and timing, will be explained by the host university.
When would the doctorate start? Start dates may differ between universities. Follow the intended start date and any flexibility stated in each official university advertisement.

Who can answer questions or help with application adjustments? Use the contact named in the relevant university advertisement for project questions, eligibility checks or reasonable adjustments to the application and selection process. For general questions about the network, contact the EMANAIRE coordinator.

You will develop your project at a host university while joining an international community of doctoral researchers and supervisors. Shared schools, methods workshops and research seminars will support your work, with planned secondments connecting your research to organisations outside academia. Employment terms and application requirements are set out in each official advertisement.
​ Project title: Machine learning-guided multiparametric optimisation of cytochrome P450 monooxygenase

The aim of this project is to simultaneously improve the activity and stability of cytochrome P450 BM3, minimizing trade-off effects and enabling a smoother transition to larger-scale application. To enable this, Lisa will develop a workflow applying high-throughput screening to generate experimental data on the enzyme's sequence and functional properties, which will be used to iteratively train a predictive machine learning model.
Background fields: s tructural biology, molecular biology
Project title: Engineering redox chains to support CYP biocatalysis

Nikola will focus on engineering fusion systems consisting of multiple enzymes to develop self-sufficient peroxygenases. A key emphasis will be placed on exploring the diversity of fusion systems by incorporating varying peroxide-producing enzymes. A wide range of industry-relevant substrates will be hydroxylated through sustainable process integration. At the end computational predictions will be accompanied by experimental results.
Background fields: biocatalysis, enzymology, molecular modelling, drug delivery systems, oncology nanotherapeutics
Project title: ML-guided evolution of peroxygenases for selective C-H oxyfunctionalisation reactions

Toni's project focuses on combining machine learning and directed evolution to engineer unspecific peroxygenases (UPOs) for selective oxyfunctionalization reactions. The project aims to integrate computational approaches with experimental enzyme engineering to explore UPO sequence–function relationships and develop improved biocatalysts.
Background fields: molecular biotechnology, enzyme engineering, directed evolution, protein engineering, machine learning, biocatalysis
Project title: Multiparametric engineering of alkene dioxygenase

Sebastián's project is focused on the characterization and improvement of non-heme iron dependent Alkene Dioxigenases, in a multiparametric approach. He will use both rational design and random mutagenesis to accomplish his goals of improving the fitness of our collection of alkene dioxigenases.
Background fields: m olecular biology, microbiology, bioinformatics
Project title: Engineering conformational dynamics and mechanism in oxygenases

The project focuses on the computationally guided design of oxygenases through the engineering of enzyme conformational dynamics and catalytic mechanism. The project aims to understand how changes in protein sequence, including mutations at residues distant from the active site can reshape the conformational ensamble of oxygenases and thereby improve activity and selectivity. In particular, Shortest Path Map (SPM) analyses are used to investigate communication networks within the enzyme and identify pathways connecting distal residues to the active site.
Background fields: b ioinformatics, machine-learning, drug discovery workflows, cheminformatics
Project title: Towards scalable, cost-effective processes for bulk chemical production of cycloalkanones

Anahita's PhD project focuses on the development of data-driven approaches for real-time monitoring, optimization, and scale-up of UPO-catalyzed biocatalytic processes. Enzymatic reactions are commonly monitored using off-line methods such as GC and HPLC. Although these methods are precise and reliable, they require regular sampling and sample preparation steps. This means the analysis will happen minutes to hours after the sampling, and human error can reduce the validity of the results. Also, dependence on off-line methods makes automation for real-time monitoring, and control almost impossible. In the project, Anahita will use Raman and FTIR spectroscopy as process analytical technology (PAT) to monitor the reaction in real-time and use it for assessing kinetic parameters, reaction mechanism, identifying critical process parameters, optimizing the reaction and process scale-up.
Background fields: biotechnology, biocatalysis, bioprocess engineering, bioengineering, process analytical technology (PAT)
Project title: Kinetic stability data collection for predictive bioprocess modelling of CYP enzymes

The main objectives of this project are to understand how dissolved oxygen affects enzyme stability in a bioprocess-realistic environment, as well as to develop a hybrid model to predict enzyme stability across different reactors and conditions. The project will involve a scale-down approach, with a focus on gathering relevant stability data for P450. The collected data will then be used for the development of a hybrid model utilizing active learning and machine learning. The initial work will focus on isolated enzymes, with the ambition of expanding the model to whole-cell systems.
Background fields: m olecular biotechnology, fermentation, biocatalysis
Project title : Process intensification of cytochrome P450 reactions in batch and continuous reactors

This project focuses on intensifying cytochrome P450-catalysed reactions in batch and continuous-flow reactors. Controlled bioreactor experiments and reaction engineering will be used to investigate how substrate supply, and the delivery of oxygen or hydrogen peroxide influence reaction efficiency and productivity. In collaboration with WP1, engineered P450 variants will be evaluated under process-relevant conditions, while the resulting kinetic and process data will contribute to modelling and machine-learning activities in WP3. Selected reactions will also be investigated in pressurized continuous-flow systems to improve oxygen availability. By identifying key process bottlenecks and developing scale-up criteria, the project aims to connect enzyme engineering with robust and scalable biocatalytic production.
Background fields : biotechnology, biochemistry, biocatalysis, bioprocess engineering, continuous-flow biocatalysis
Project title: Process development and optimization of dioxygenase catalysed biotransformation

The project is process development and optimisation of dioxygenase-catalysed biotransformation based on the conversion of isoeugenol to vanillin, focusing on biocatalyst operational stability under bioreactor conditions. The research will combine experimental biocatalyst development, kinetic characterization, mathematical modelling, and in silico process intensification and validation.
Background fields: e nzyme bioprocess, reaction engineering, process intensification, machine learning
Project title: Continuous flow oxyfunctionalisations of allylic substrates catalysed by UPOs

The aim of this project is to develop efficient and reusable unspecific peroxygenase (UPO) biocatalysts for selective oxyfunctionalization. Nektaria will combine protein engineering and process engineering to improve UPO activity, selectivity, stability, and reusability for allylic oxyfunctionalization. Diverse UPOs and allylic substrates will be screened to identify promising enzyme–substrate combinations, while enzyme immobilization, continuous-flow operation, and controlled H₂O₂ supply will be explored to enhance overall catalytic and process performance, enabling more efficient and sustainable oxyfunctionalization chemistry.
Background fields: biotechnology, biochemistry, biocatalysis, protein engineering, and bioprocess engineering
Project title: Machine learning-based tools for multiparametric enzyme optimisation

Daniela's project focuses on developing machine learning-based tools for multiparametric enzyme optimisation. Building on protein mutational datasets generated in-house for a range of enzymes, as well as public protein databases, she will explore and compare state-of-the-art data representation techniques to build next-generation data-driven models for engineering properties such as enzyme activity, selectivity, stability and solubility.
Background fields: computational chemistry, bioinformatics, molecular dynamics
Project title: Development of machine learned coarse grained force fields for computational enzyme design

Filippo works on machine-learned force-fields for enzyme systems — neural network models that learn from reference data the potential energy surface governing how these proteins move. He is particularly interested in coarse-grained models, which enable the simulation of long-timescale dynamics. He is also interested in explainability and interpretability methods, which make machine-learning models transparent rather than black boxes: understanding what the network has learned about the underlying physics and why it produces a given prediction, both to trust the simulations and to extract mechanistic insight into how enzymes work.
Project title: Development of ML-based tools for analysis and engineering protein dynamics

Tillman’s project focuses on developing machine-learning tools to analyse and engineer protein dynamics. These movements and conformational changes play a central role in how enzymes function. The project aims to move beyond static protein structures by developing efficient methods to predict, understand, and deliberately modify dynamic behaviour. He will also develop AI-assisted workflows that support the progression from researching a target protein and computationally screening designs to prioritizing candidates for experimental validation. The broader goal is to establish protein dynamics as a practical component of protein design, enabling useful enzyme variants to be identified with fewer experiments and less computation.
Background fields: machine learning, bioinformatics, scientific software engineering, agentic workflows
Project title: EVB- and AI-guided Engineering of Unspecific Peroxygenases (UPOs) for Selective Benzylic Hydroxylation

Biya's project combines computational methods and machine learning to engineer unspecific peroxygenases (UPOs) for selective benzylic C–H hydroxylation, a reaction that competes with off-target epoxidation and overoxidation. Towards this, she will build calibrated EVB/QM/MM models of the enzyme's reaction mechanism to understand how its structure governs this selectivity, and use these insights to propose targeted mutations. The collected simulation data will then be used to develop an uncertainty-aware active learning model that prioritises the enzyme variants most worth testing, rather than screening them all. The project also extends into process engineering, modelling how the enzyme performs under real operating conditions to support its future use at an industrial scale. This combination of mechanistic simulation and data-driven prediction is intended to identify UPO variants and operating conditions that improve selectivity and productivity, with fewer experiments than conventional screening would require.
Background fields: theoretical and computational chemistry, molecular dynamics simulation
Project title: Hybrid models for data-driven bioprocess optimization

Athina's project focuses on developing novel machine learning methods for the design and optimization of bioprocesses in biocatalysis. The objective is to develop an algorithmic toolbox for bioprocess optimization, scale-down process development, control and transfer learning across different processes. The optimization aims to maximize process outcome and minimize experimental resources. Regarding scale-up and scale-down, variable mismatches arise between scales, leading to different effects on the process. For control, the goal is to achieve real-time control under uncertainty, accounting for the nonlinear and dynamic nature of the system. The model will be applied to UPO, CYP and DO production processes, using hybrid models as the modeling method.
Background fields: bioprocess engineering, hybrid modeling, machine learning

DCs will contribute to interdisciplinary projects addressing challenges such as biofilm-related infections, real-time diagnostics and targeted antimicrobial therapies.
A unique MSCA doctoral training experience

HEAL4WARD provides a comprehensive doctoral training programme aligned with the MSCA Doctoral Network model, combining scientific excellence with structured skills development. Selected candidates will benefit from:
Full-time employment contracts with competitive salaries and social benefits in line with MSCA regulations
Joint supervision by leading academic, clinical and industrial partners
Access to high-quality research infrastructures and interdisciplinary expertise

A key feature of the programme is its strong emphasis on mobility and international exposure. Throughout the programme, each DC will undertake secondments with other organisations within the HEAL4WARD consortium, including academic institutions, clinical environments and industrial partners. These secondments are designed to extend learning beyond the host institution, allowing candidates to gain practical experience in different sectors, strengthen interdisciplinary collaboration and better understand the translation of research into real-world healthcare solutions. DCs will be hosted across multiple European countries, including institutions in Ireland, Spain, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and other partner locations, reflecting the network’s broad geographic coverage.

In addition to their individual research projects, DCs will participate in a comprehensive network-wide training programme designed to complement their scientific development. This includes thematic training schools and specialised workshops, as well as dedicated courses on transferable skills such as scientific communication, entrepreneurship, intellectual property management and research ethics. The programme also facilitates active engagement with stakeholders across academia, healthcare systems and industry, ensuring that candidates develop a well-rounded skill set and are equipped for diverse career pathways both within and beyond academia.

Genome – GENerative and connected intelligence for 6G Open ManagemEnt
GENOME: GENerative and connected intelligence for 6G Open ManagemEnt

AI and large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to handle complex tasks across many fields. In network management, they offer powerful tools to automate operations, improve efficiency, and optimise performance. Supported by the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions programme, the GENOME project aims to design, develop, and test LLM-based solutions for the autonomous management of different network domains. Using task-agnostic network functions and intent-based networking, it intends to create an intelligence framework that enables coordination, rapid learning, and conflict-free decision-making, strengthening both efficiency and resilience.
GENOME sets the following ambitious research objectives (ROs):
RO-A. Design GenAI/scalable mixture of experts (MoE)-based models for network management, especially at edge.
RO-B. Design methods for automatic configuration generation of softwarized edge and RAN network segments and task planning.
RO-C. Develop new multi-agent communication-based protocols in the future-proof 6G O-RAN .

RO-D. Design transparent and resilient AI functions by developing AI act-aligned in-hoc XAI methods for LLMs/SLMs in 6G O-RAN as well as building context for AI security systems via LLMs and Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) .

MEDIculous REMeDy offers 15 fully funded doctoral positions through the European Union's Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) Doctoral Networks program. Throughout the program, doctoral candidates benefit from dedicated supervision, personalized career development and seven Network Training Events hosted at partner institutions across Europe. The training combines advanced scientific and computational courses, transferable skills training, leadership development, science communication workshops and extensive networking opportunities with experts from academia, healthcare, industry, public institutions and patient organizations. should demonstrate strong motivation for metabolic health research and enjoy working collaboratively in an international and multidisciplinary environment.

At MEDIculous REMeDy, we are committed to a fair, transparent and inclusive recruitment process, in line with the European Charter for Researchers and the Code of Conduct for the Recruitment of Researchers. All applications are evaluated through an Open, Transparent and Merit-based Recruitment (OTM-R) using standardized criteria to ensure consistency, objectivity and equal opportunities throughout the selection process. We actively promote an inclusive environment and welcome applications regardless of gender, nationality, age, religion, sexual orientation or disability. The applications are assessed according to the following steps:
The project coordination team verifies that applicants fulfil the MSCA eligibility criteria and the admission requirements of the respective host institution.

Each eligible application is independently evaluated by three MEDIculous REMeDy project leaders. Applications are assessed using standardized evaluation criteria covering academic excellence, scientific motivation, research aptitude, independence and future impact.

The highest-ranked candidates are invited to give a short online presentation of their previous research, followed by a structured interview with the project supervisors to evaluate scientific aptitude, motivation and suitability for the doctoral project.

The final ranking is based on the written application and interview scores. Successful candidates receive an offer from the recruiting institution, while additional highly ranked applicants are placed on a reserve list in case positions become available.

DC9 Modelling of the dynamic response for offshore wind farms - This position is now filled

The combination of a long coastline, shallow water, and offshore wind makes the UK one of the best locations in the world for wind power. As of 2023, the UK has over 11,000 wind turbines generating 30 GW of power, which accounts for almost 30% of the UK electricity supply. The UK Government has committed to increase the offshore capacity to 50 GW by 2030. Despite these significant benefits and enthusiasm for wind power, there are some serious challenges, which have become apparently in the last two decades 1) Clusters of turbines can produce powerful standing waves, in both air and seawater, severely affecting wildlife and radar and sonar operations. 2) Wind turbines are gyroscopic systems that possess highly complex chiral vibrational modes. DC9 will develop novel mathematical models to predict the dynamic phenomena arising in offshore wind farms and further model the acoustic waves generated by individual, and clusters of, wind turbines to help quantify the effect on wildlife, including birds, marine mammals, and fish.

LowDataML is launching an ambitious recruitment programme for 10 Doctoral Candidate (DC) positions across leading European institutions and industry partners. These positions are part of a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) Doctoral Network focused on Low Data Machine Learning for Sustainable Chemical Sciences, offering cutting-edge research opportunities at the intersection of artificial intelligence, chemistry, and drug discovery. Each DC will enrol in a PhD programme and benefit from a structured training plan combining academic excellence, industrial exposure, and interdisciplinary collaboration.

Recruitment will follow the European Charter for Researchers and the Code of Conduct, ensuring transparency, gender equality, and non-discrimination. Candidates must hold a Master’s degree (or equivalent) in a relevant discipline and demonstrate strong motivation and scientific potential. Each DC will sign a 3-year contract with the host institution, receive a competitive MSCA salary (including mobility and family allowances), and participate in secondments at partner organisations. Applications will be advertised globally through EURAXESS and other channels, and selection will involve a fair, inclusive process aligned with Horizon Europe standards.
Explore the positions below to learn more about each opportunity:
DC1: Designing necroptosis/NAFLD modulators with one-shot learning (Mentor: Tiago Rodrigues, University of Lisbon, Portugal)
Host: FARM-ID, Faculty of Pharmacy, University of Lisbon Duration: 36 months | PhD enrolment: Yes
This PhD project will explore few-shot learning and anomaly detection in medicinal chemistry to design novel modulators targeting necroptosis and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).

Key objectives: • Expand the ligand space of RIPK3 and prioritise molecules for synthesis using advanced ML strategies • Apply transfer learning (LSTMs) and Siamese neural networks for bioactivity prediction • Develop generative models and anomaly detection approaches for de novo molecule design • Evaluate up to 10 candidate molecules through synthesis and biological validation
The candidate will also contribute to building curated datasets and sustainable drug design workflows.
Planned secondments: • 3 months at TUE for deep learning expertise • 3 months at IBM for LLMs in drug design • 6 months at AC for synthesis of small molecules
DC2: Agentic AI for drug discovery (Mentor: Samuel Genheden, AstraZeneca, Sweden)
Host: AZ Duration: 36 months | PhD enrolment: Yes

This PhD project will focus on introducing novel reaction types into retrosynthesis planning tools using machine learning models trained on chemoinformatics rules and ab initio data. The goal is to enhance predictive capabilities for synthetic pathways by combining computational chemistry and AI-driven approaches.

Key objectives: • Develop automatic pipelines for ab initio calculations of novel reaction types • Extract descriptors from chemical reactions to train ML models for retrosynthesis • Build prediction models (retro, forward, and condition) to assess feasibility and optimise reaction conditions • Integrate novel reaction types into multi-step retrosynthesis algorithms and evaluate their impact
The candidate will also contribute to creating open-source tools for deriving ML models from ab initio data and validating selected reaction types experimentally.

Planned secondments: • 5 months at EPFL to advance deep learning methods for synthetic pathway prediction • 3 months at ARQ to develop QM/ML approaches • 4 months at BGU to strengthen skills in synthetic chemistry

DC3: Tuning ADC payload release with active learning (Mentor: Gonçalo Bernardes, University of Cambridge, UK)
Host: UCAM Duration: 36 months | PhD enrolment: Yes

This PhD project aims to optimise the release of payloads in antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) by tuning linker structures and payload properties using active learning approaches. The focus will be on controlling payload release through modulation of pKa values and chemical derivatisation strategies, improving therapeutic precision in cancer treatment.

Key objectives: • Develop an active learning loop to predict and optimise payload release from ADCs • Establish correlations between linker structure, payload pKa, and release rates in cells • Implement ML models to identify optimal substitution patterns for controlled release • Validate predictions through synthesis and experimental testing in vitro and in vivo
The candidate will also contribute to applying these strategies in real-world scenarios, including bioconjugation for acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) therapy.

Host: TUE Duration: 36 months | PhD enrolment: Yes

This PhD project will explore causal deep learning as an innovative approach to drug discovery, focusing on identifying novel PPARγ partial agonists. By leveraging small datasets and reusable causal relations, the project aims to overcome limitations of current algorithms and enable robust, generalisable models for low-data scenarios.

Key objectives: • Investigate how causality can be incorporated into molecular machine learning • Develop causal deep learning models for structure–activity prediction and ligand-protein interactions • Apply few-shot learning to discover new PPARγ partial agonists using commercially available libraries • Validate causal inference and refine models through iterative experimental cycles
The candidate will also contribute to designing easy-to-use ML tools for medicinal chemistry and generating insights for hit-to-lead optimisation.

This PhD project addresses one of the main bottlenecks in drug discovery: predicting the outcome of chemical reactions. Using few-shot learning and deep learning approaches, the goal is to improve reactivity prediction in low-data regimes, enabling sustainable and efficient synthetic planning.

MLCARE – Machine Learning Computational Advancements for peRsonalized mEdicine (HORIZON – MSCA – 2024 – DN – 101226456 – MLCARE)
Machine Learning Computational Advancements for peRsonalized mEdicine (HORIZON – MSCA – 2024 – DN – 101226456 – MLCARE)

Precision medicine represents a paradigm shift in healthcare, transitioning from generalized treatment strategies to highly personalized care. This transformation is driven by rapid advancements in digital technologies, which generate massive volumes of data from diverse sources, including genomic sequences , high-resolution imaging, wearable devices, and electronic health records (EHRs). However, despite an annual estimate of 50 petabytes of data generated per hospital , only a fraction is utilized effectively. Harnessing this untapped potential offers a transformative opportunity to uncover novel disease mechanisms and deliver more precise and effective therapeutic interventions.

The MLCare project seeks to revolutionize precision medicine by developing cutting-edge AI solutions that integrate genomic, clinical, and environmental data into holistic, multimodal patient representations. Through innovative approaches such as Foundation Models and advanced generative AI methods, MLCare will address critical challenges in processing complex, high-dimensional, and multimodal datasets. Emphasis will be placed on ensuring the trustworthiness , explainability, and security of AI applications to support real-world clinical decision-making.

A core mission of MLCare is to train a new generation of 14 interdisciplinary researchers with expertise spanning AI, computational biology, and healthcare . The program will equip doctoral candidates with the technical, analytical, and ethical skills needed to lead the future of patient-centered, AI-driven medicine. By combining state-of-the-art research with a comprehensive training program, MLCare aims to set new standards in personalized healthcare, ensuring equitable, data-driven solutions that improve outcomes across diverse populations. This project is poised to position Europe at the forefront of global innovation in precision medicine , delivering a timely and impactful response to evolving healthcare challenges.

The network’s science is carried by 15 connected PhD projects. Each is hosted by a different group, co-supervised across institutions, and linked to a partner. They are designed to feed one another: data and tools from one project become the inputs for several others.

Can a machine learn to recognize a real microprotein gene from its DNA alone? This project builds AI models that predict which short ORFs are genuinely translated, trained on data from across the network and released as open tools for the wider community.
Co-supervisor: Uwe Ohler (Max Delbrück Center, Berlin)

Can a machine learn to recognize a real microprotein gene from its DNA alone? Across the tree of life, genomes contain thousands of short open reading frames that might encode proteins, but most annotation tools were never designed to flag sequences this small. The result is that many genuine microprotein genes have been missed entirely.

This project builds a foundation model for smORF detection: an AI system that integrates mRNA sequence, cellular context, and ribosome profiling data to predict translation at codon-level resolution. The model learns from data across the ORFeus network, including dual host-pathogen datasets from DC4, rare translation events from DC3, and genetic variant information from DC12, and is iteratively refined as experimental validation comes in from groups across the consortium. The goal is not just a better predictor, but a set of open, reusable tools that the wider community can build on.
All models and predictions will be released through the ORFeome platform and HuggingFace. X
AI and machine learning, ribosome profiling data integration, cross-species computational genomics.
Reading translation one molecule at a time

What can single molecules tell us about translation that bulk methods cannot? This project combines single-molecule translation data with computational modeling to map which ORFs are translated from individual RNA isoforms, and how transcript structure and RNA modifications shape that choice.
Supervisor: Uwe Ohler (Max Delbrück Center, Berlin)

Standard ribosome profiling gives a population-level view: it tells you that a particular ORF is translated in a sample, but not which specific RNA molecule is being read, or how different transcript forms from the same gene carry different proteins. Many smORFs sit outside reference catalogs altogether, and some may be produced together from a single polycistronic transcript. This project goes beyond population averages to resolve translation at the level of individual RNA molecules and their isoforms.

The project builds on RiboSTAMP, a technique that marks translating ribosomes by fusing a cytidine deaminase to a ribosomal protein, combined with Oxford Nanopore long-read direct RNA sequencing to connect translation information directly to full-length transcript structure. The emphasis is computational: you will develop multi-omics methods that combine RiboSTAMP with ribosome profiling and polysome profiling to map translation onto specific RNA isoforms, and use RNA foundation models to quantify how RNA structure and modifications such as m6A shape which ORFs are translated. You will also help validate RiboSTAMP in the lab under normal and stress conditions, and test whether it can be adapted to single cells.

Results inform work across the network, from AI-based smORF prediction in DC1 and rare translation events in DC3 to RNA modification effects in DC7 and single-cell translation in DC9, and feed into the shared ORFeome resource. A secondment of around three months at Oxford Nanopore Technologies focuses on optimizing direct RNA sequencing and analysis workflows for RiboSTAMP.
Bioinformatics, Machine learning, Post-transcriptional gene regulation, Long-read sequencing, Genomics, Proteomics
Industry partner for secondment: Oxford Nanopore Technologies (UK)
Finding rare proteins in a sea of data

Most translation events are common enough to detect in a single experiment, but what about the rare ones? This project mines more than 15,000 public ribosome profiling datasets to find translation events that only appear under specific conditions or in specific species.

Most translation events are common enough to detect in a single ribosome profiling experiment. But many of the most interesting microproteins may be translated only under very specific conditions: in a particular tissue, during a moment of stress, or in a species no one has profiled yet. These are the hardest to find, and the most likely to be missing from current catalogs.

This project takes a data-driven approach. Rather than running new experiments one at a time, it brings together more than 15,000 publicly available ribosome profiling datasets and mines them at scale, asking which short open reading frames show evidence of translation across conditions, species, and cell states. The challenge is both computational and methodological: different labs use different protocols and organisms, and separating real signals from technical noise across such a heterogeneous collection requires new approaches.

The project builds on the Valen group’s ORFik framework and connects directly to RiboSeq.Org, the community data platform co-developed with the Baranov group at UCC. Validated rare events are cross-referenced with immunopeptidomics data from DC11 and DC15 to check whether cryptic translation products reach the cell surface.
large-scale ribosome profiling data aggregation, computational method development, cross-species comparative genomics.
Industry partner for secondment: EIRNA Bio (Ireland)
Institute of Cancer Research · London, UK

When a bacterium infects a cell, both host and pathogen produce microproteins. This project maps that landscape using dual proteomics and ribosome profiling, asking which microproteins shape the course of infection.
Supervisor: Jyoti Choudhary (Institute of Cancer Research, London)

When a bacterium infects a cell, both host and pathogen are translating proteins, and both may be producing microproteins that have never been catalogued. This project maps that dual landscape in the context of enteric infection, using Citrobacter rodentium as a model pathogen.

The project combines advanced dual proteomics (capturing host and pathogen proteins simultaneously) with ribosome profiling to build a time-resolved picture of microprotein dynamics across three stages of infection, from initial contact through to established disease. Proximity labelling (BioID) is used to identify which host and pathogen microproteins interact with each other during infection, and thermal proteome profiling (in collaboration with DC10) validates these interactions.
The result is a comprehensive ORFeome dataset of infection-associated microproteins, which also serves as a biologically relevant input for the antigen presentation studies in WP3.
dual host-pathogen proteomics, ribosome profiling (Ribo-Seq), proximity labelling (BioID), thermal proteome profiling, mouse infection models.
Capturing the proteins cells send to each other

Many microproteins are secreted from cells, but current methods largely miss them. This project develops chemical tagging approaches to capture secreted microproteins and identify the cell-surface receptors they bind to.
Co-supervisor: Jyoti Choudhary (Institute of Cancer Research, London)

Many microproteins are secreted from cells, where they may act as signalling molecules or interact with receptors on neighbouring cells. But current proteomic methods largely miss them because they are small, present at low concentrations, and quickly diluted in cell culture media. This project develops new chemical biology approaches to capture them.

The project uses bioorthogonal non-canonical amino acid labelling to introduce minimal chemical handles into microproteins, combined with crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) to capture secreted microproteins at the moment they bind their cell-surface receptors. The approach is applied to co-culture models of the tumour microenvironment, where cancer cells communicate with immune and stromal cells through signals that may include microproteins no one has seen before.
The resulting atlas of secreted microproteins feeds into the binder design work in DC6 and provides candidate targets for the immunotherapy-focused projects in DC14 and DC15.
bioorthogonal chemistry, non-canonical amino acid labelling, crosslinking mass spectrometry (XL-MS), cancer cell co-culture models.

Once you find a microprotein, how do you work out what it does? This project uses computational protein design to create synthetic molecules that bind specific microproteins and switch their activity on or off.

Once a microprotein is identified, how do you find out what it does? One powerful approach is to design a synthetic molecule that binds it specifically and can switch its activity on or off. This project uses computational protein design to create such binders for microproteins identified across the ORFeus network.

The project starts with a consortium-prioritized list of 20 target microproteins, expresses and purifies them, and performs biophysical characterization. It then uses AI-based design tools, including AlphaFold3 and RoseTTAFold, to computationally design high-affinity synthetic binders. These are iteratively refined using structural and biophysical data from DC10 and validated using binding assays and, in collaboration with DC5, cellular assays that test whether the binder actually modulates the microprotein’s function.
The structural models, binder sequences, and biophysical data are contributed to the ORFeome platform as a shared resource for functional validation.
computational protein design (AlphaFold3, RoseTTAFold), protein expression and purification, biophysical characterization (SEC-MALS, biolayer interferometry), cellular assays.

Long non-coding RNAs were long assumed not to make proteins, but some of them do. This project investigates the rules that govern when and how ribosomes translate these unexpected transcripts, focusing on neuronal development.
Co-supervisor: M. Mar Albà (Hospital del Mar Research Institute, Barcelona)

Long non-coding RNAs were assumed, by definition, not to encode proteins. But ribosome profiling has shown that many of them carry small open reading frames that are translated into microproteins, most of which are missing from standard reference catalogs. Which lncRNAs are translated, and how the features of each transcript control how efficiently and where translation happens, are open questions at the heart of dark proteome biology.

This project investigates the rules that govern when and how ribosomes translate lncRNAs, using the differentiation of human SH-SY5Y cells into neurons as a model system. Neuronal differentiation is a dynamic process in which translation is tightly regulated, which makes it well suited to catching these rules at work. The project uses TCP-Seq (translation complex profile sequencing) to map how ribosomes scan along transcripts, and long-read direct RNA sequencing to resolve the full-length transcript structures involved. Candidate regulatory motifs and factors are then tested with mini-gene reporters and siRNA knockdowns, building toward a map of ribosome scanning across lncRNAs.

The collaboration with M. Mar Albà in Barcelona adds an evolutionary dimension: if a translation feature or microprotein has been conserved across species, that is strong evidence it matters. The partnership with Oxford Nanopore Technologies, where you will spend around three months, contributes long-read sequencing expertise and the chance to co-develop new translation profiling methods based on direct RNA sequencing.
ribosome profiling (Ribo-Seq, Poly-Ribo-Seq), TCP-Seq, long-read direct RNA sequencing, evolutionary genomics.

Evolution leaves traces. If a microprotein has been conserved across species, it is more likely to matter. This project uses evolutionary analysis and functional screens to predict which newly discovered microproteins are biologically important.
Supervisor: M. Mar Albà (Hospital del Mar Research Institute, Barcelona)

Evolution leaves traces. If a microprotein has been conserved across species over millions of years, it is very likely to do something important. If it appeared recently in evolutionary time, it may still be functional, but the evidence is harder to read. This project uses evolutionary analysis to predict which newly discovered microproteins matter.

The project builds computational models that integrate ribosome profiling data, phylostratigraphy (to estimate evolutionary age), and genetic variant data from population databases like gnomAD and the UK Biobank. The models predict which microproteins show signs of evolutionary constraint, and therefore which are most likely to be functional. Top candidates are then validated experimentally using CRISPR-Cas9 screens in cancer cell lines, testing whether their disruption affects cell growth, drug resistance, or DNA repair.
Evolutionary constraint data also feeds back into DC1’s prediction models, and functionally validated microproteins are prioritized for further study in DC13 and the translational projects in WP3.
evolutionary genomics, phylostratigraphy, computational modelling, CRISPR-Cas9 functional screens, integration with population genetics databases.

Translation, one cell at a time

Different cells in the same tissue can translate the same gene differently. This project develops a new method that combines CRISPR editing with single-cell ribosome profiling to study translation regulation one cell at a time.
Supervisor: Alexander van Oudenaarden (Hubrecht Institute, Utrecht)

Different cells in the same tissue can translate the same gene differently. A tumour is not one cell type but many, and the microproteins that matter in one subpopulation may be absent in another. Understanding this heterogeneity requires translation profiling at single-cell resolution, something that has only recently become technically feasible.

This project establishes a new “ribo-perturb-seq” framework that combines CRISPR-based editing with single-cell ribosome profiling. The approach adapts Perturb-seq vector designs so that guide RNAs and translation profiles can be read out simultaneously from the same individual cell. After validation in K562 and RPE-1 cell lines, the technology is applied to organoid models of neural development in collaboration with DC7, investigating how smORF variants affect translation regulation during differentiation.
Isoform-level translation data from DC2 informs the single-cell analysis frameworks, and top candidates from DC7’s lncRNA translation studies are functionally validated at single-cell resolution.
single-cell ribosome profiling, CRISPR Perturb-seq, organoid models, computational single-cell analysis.

How does removing a single microprotein change the behavior of a whole proteome? This project uses thermal proteome profiling in bacteria to measure how protein stability and interactions shift when a microprotein is absent, building a functional map of the microproteome.

How does removing a single microprotein change the behaviour of a whole proteome? Most approaches to studying protein function focus on one protein at a time, but thermal proteome profiling (TPP) offers something different: a proteome-wide readout of how protein stability and interactions shift when a gene is disrupted.

This project applies TPP systematically to 20 microprotein deletion strains of Salmonella enterica across five different growth conditions, building a comprehensive functional map of the bacterial microproteome. Changes in stability point to protein-protein interactions, and the most confident hits are validated using biophysical methods and integrated with structure predictions from AlphaFold and RoseTTAFold in collaboration with DC6.
The resulting workflows are designed to be reusable: adapted for host-pathogen interaction studies with DC4, and providing biophysical data that informs the binder design work in DC6.
thermal proteome profiling (TPP), Salmonella genetics, mass spectrometry, biophysical validation (biolayer interferometry, SEC-MALS), structural prediction.

HPV rewrites the host cell’s RNA landscape, and some of the resulting hybrid transcripts may encode new proteins. This project maps non-canonical translation in HPV-driven cancers and tests whether the resulting peptides can be recognized by the immune system.
Co-supervisor: Sebastiaan van Heesch (Princess Máxima Center, Utrecht)

HPV rewrites the host cell’s RNA landscape. When the viral genome integrates into the human genome, it can create hybrid transcripts that fuse viral and human sequences, and some of these may encode proteins that have never been catalogued. If those proteins are displayed on the cell surface, the immune system could potentially recognize them as foreign, making them attractive targets for immunotherapy.

This project maps non-canonical translation in HPV-driven cancers. Using long- and short-read RNA-Seq combined with ribosome profiling in HPV-positive reference cell lines and head-and-neck squamous cell carcinoma cell lines, the project identifies hybrid viral-human transcripts and determines which of them are translated. Proteomics and immunopeptidomics then confirm whether the resulting peptides are processed and presented on HLA molecules. The immunogenicity of the most promising candidates is tested using T-cell assays.

The result is an “HPV Immune Map” of non-canonical translation and antigen presentation, contributing validated peptide candidates to DC15’s predictive modelling and informing the regulatory studies in DC14.
ribosome profiling (Ribo-Seq), long- and short-read RNA-Seq, immunopeptidomics, proteomics, T-cell immunogenicity assays.

Common genetic variants can change which proteins a cell makes, even outside the known gene catalog. This project studies how variation in non-coding regions alters translation, and which of these changes are relevant in cancer.
Co-supervisor: Alexander van Oudenaarden (Hubrecht Institute, Utrecht)

Common genetic variants can change which proteins a cell makes, even outside the known gene catalog. A single nucleotide change in a non-coding region might create a new start codon, eliminate one, or alter how the ribosome navigates a complex transcript. Most of these effects are invisible to standard genome-wide association studies, because the affected ORFs are not annotated.

This project investigates how genetic variants in non-coding regions alter translation, using Ribosome Decision Graphs (RDGs), a framework developed in the Baranov group for representing the complexity of eukaryotic translation. The project adapts RDGs to be genotype-specific, integrating data from population databases (UK BioBank, gnomAD) and new ribosome profiling data from DepMap cancer cell lines. With DC3, it builds an integrated map of translation diversity by identifying where variant-triggered and naturally rare translation events overlap.
The ultimate goal is a catalogue of cancer-relevant translation-altering variants, advancing the field’s ability to interpret non-coding variants identified in patient genomes.
ribosome profiling, Ribosome Decision Graphs, population genetics, computational genomics, DepMap cell line analysis.

Wrong amino acids, new immune targets

What happens when cancer cells start reading their genome in unexpected ways? This project studies how tumour cells switch on a hidden layer of protein coding under stress, and what the resulting dark proteome means for cancer biology and immunotherapy. The work runs alongside ILLUMINE, the Cancer Grand Challenges project on the dark proteome.
Supervisor: Sebastiaan van Heesch (Princess Máxima Center, Utrecht)
Co-supervisor: Reuven Agami (Netherlands Cancer Institute, Amsterdam)

What happens when cancer cells start reading their genome in unexpected ways? Under the metabolic stress that is typical of a tumour and its microenvironment, cells can switch on a hidden layer of protein coding, translating sequences that are normally silent and producing proteins through non-canonical mechanisms. A central question is how this process works mechanistically, and what the resulting dark proteome means for cancer biology and for the immune system’s ability to recognise tumour cells.

This project studies non-canonical translation in cancer, with particular interest in how cellular stress, including amino acid deprivation, drives the production of aberrant microproteins. Using ribosome profiling, proteomics, and immunopeptidomics, the project identifies these proteins and asks whether they are presented on HLA molecules where the immune system can find them. The work runs alongside ILLUMINE, the Cancer Grand Challenges project on the dark proteome, and will integrate and collaborate with it where the science aligns.
The precise focus will be shaped together with the successful candidate and the supervisory team.
ribosome profiling (Ribo-Seq), mass-spectrometry proteomics, immunopeptidomics, computational analysis.
